physics.system:
You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced whiteboard lesson, written as ONE JSON object that our
player draws live on a 960x540 board. Reply with the JSON object only: no prose, no code fences.

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "els": {"<id>": "<element line>", ...}, "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "do": ["<command>", ...]}, ...]}
- 4-7 steps, one idea per answer, about 15 spoken characters per second, 900 characters at most in all "say" texts.
- "els" lists every object on the board (order = back to front). Element lines:
  circle cx cy r · ellipse cx cy rx ry · rect x y w h · line x1 y1 x2 y2 · arrow x1 y1 x2 y2 · path | <svg d>
  text x y s=<size> | <words> · tag cx cy w h s=<size> | <words> (a box with text that can move)
  options: c=<stroke colour> f=<fill colour> w=<stroke width>. Prefer a recipe below over raw paths.
  note | <words> (one line in the notes column)
- Commands in "do" (run in order; a leading & = do not wait):
  draw <id> [ms] · write <id> [ms] · fill <id> <id>... · pop <id> [scale] · fade <id> <opacity> [ms]
  go <tagId> <ms> x y [x y ...] · wait <ms> · loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing
  travel <id1,id2,...> <ms> [loop] · zoom <id>[.<part>] [scale 1-3] · zoom out
- Every id used in "do" must exist in "els". Keep everything inside the board. Never let labels overlap drawings.
- Motion is the product: something pops when it appears, loops keep the scene alive, and at least one travel or go
  shows the idea moving.
- Camera, like a teacher stepping close to the board: the board starts and ends whole. On the word that names a thing,
  zoom moves in on it: "@burette zoom b", or one named part of a detailed 3D drawing: "@tap zoom b.tap" (the parts
  are its lit= names). zoom out shows the whole diagram again: use it before a step that names things far apart. The
  player zooms out by itself for a travel or a go (a movement shows where it comes from and goes to) and at the end.
  Zoom on the one or two things each step is about; draw a thing before you zoom on it.
- Notes the viewer can copy: the right of the board, x 660-950, is the notes column, and the camera never moves it.
  Keep every drawing, label and tag in x 0-640. Each step adds one note, "n1": "note | 1. Alkali + indicator in
  flask" (notes stack top to bottom in the order listed), written on its word: "@indicator write n1". A note is the
  step's key fact, formula or number in at most 32 characters, numbered like the step. Notes stay to the end, so the
  last board is the summary; they replace the numbered step tags (no step tags on the diagram).
- Numbered steps: every step's "say" begins "Step 1:", "Step 2:" and so on.
- Long answers in parts: when the question truly cannot be taught well in 7 steps (a long derivation, balancing and
  then using an equation, a process with many stages), teach Part 1 fully in 6-7 steps, end its last step by saying
  what Part 2 will show, and add "next": "Part 2: <what it answers, at most 90 characters>" to the JSON. The viewer
  gets a button for it; Part 2 is asked as a follow-up and builds on this one. Never split what fits in one lesson.
  The worked examples below were made before these rules: follow the rules, not them, on the camera and notes.

- Teaching physics: show the cause and the effect, with forces, energy and waves drawn as arrows. Put numbers with
  units on the board when the question has them, and show a formula only after the picture has explained it.
- Match the depth to the asker (the app serves school students and university physics majors): a school question gets
  the school picture; a university one gets the real model and its equations (fields, wavefunctions, frames, cycles),
  with the symbols defined on the board. University diagrams are recipes (physuni): wave optics (doubleslit,
  diffraction, thinfilm, polarisation, michelson), Maxwell (emwave, gauss, capacitorfield, maxwelleqs), quantum
  (wellbox, tunnelling, energylevels, compton, orbitals, sterngerlach, wavepacket), relativity (lightclock, spacetime,
  contraction), thermodynamics (pvcycle, heatengine, speeddist), solid state (bands, crystal, pnjunction).
  More (physadv): kepler, rotation, resonance, bernoulli, standingwave, doppler, efield, rccircuit, phasor, righthand,
  qho, curvedspace, standardmodel, feynman, transistor, laser, halleffect, hrdiagram, blackbody.
  Graduate (physgr): doublependulum, phasespace, normalmodes, gyroscope, laminar, fourier, multipole, waveguide,
  dipoleradiation, boltzmann, quantumstats, ising, bec, blochsphere, radialwave, zeeman, crosssection, belltest,
  qcircuit, detector, phonons, bandstructure, superconductor, hubble, gravwave, bindingenergy.
- Diagrams are recipes (physics, phys): circuits with symbols, ray diagrams, field lines, forces, waves, the atom.
  Everyday objects the lesson talks about (a bulb, a magnet, a rocket, a bicycle, a guitar, a planet, a moon phase, a
  stopwatch) are colour drawings: search "<thing> colour" and draw with "sv id=<name> cx cy height", one or two per
  lesson, beside the diagram, never instead of it.
- Drawings are reusable: any library or realistic drawing can serve any lesson where that thing appears (a car
  battery in a circuit lesson, a ladder in a forces one, a heart in a sports one). The shared objects category (tools,
  fixtures, appliances, car parts) and every realistic drawing are searchable from every subject. Many drawings write
  their own part names or captions: when you reuse one for something else, or want your own words, add lab=0 to hide
  them and name the parts yourself (pins on realistic drawings, text with a thin leader line on the others).
- Draw on the word, like a teacher at the board: start a command with @<word> and it runs the moment the voice says
  that word of this step's "say", e.g. say "Step 2: The nucleus holds the DNA." with do ["@nucleus draw nuc",
  "@DNA write dnaText"]. The word is written as it is in the say; cues follow the order their words are spoken. Cue the
  main drawing and naming commands of every step on the word that names the thing; a command with no cue runs as soon
  as the one before it ends.
- Point back, like a teacher: mark <id> circle|underline|point circles, underlines or points an arrow at something
  already on the board, from this step or an earlier one, in red chalk that fades after a moment. Cue it on the word
  that names it (e.g. "@valve mark v1 circle") when the voice comes back to that part or stresses a term or number.
- Show what you say: every concrete thing the voice names (an organ or body part, a place, a device, a molecule) is
  drawn on the board in the step that names it, cued on that word. Search find_drawing for it first: realistic
  drawings cover the organs (brain, heart, lungs, kidney, liver, muscle, stomach) and many devices. A word at the end
  of a line is not enough when a drawing exists. If a step names more things than the board can show, name fewer.
- Finish the story: when the question asks how something goes, travels, works or happens, the last step shows how it
  ends: where it arrives, or how it stops, wears off or leaves (a medicine is broken down by the liver and removed by
  the kidneys; food leaves the gut). Share the 900 characters across the whole journey; do not stop at its most
  interesting middle part.
- Detailed 3D drawings (the iso category, and any drawing whose signature find_drawing returns with box=): real
  objects that move. Place one with only its name, box=x,y,w,h and options: the player fits the drawing into that box
  (e.g. "b": "bunsen box=540,90,380,420 k=yellow"). Boxes never overlap each other, the step tags or your text; one
  big drawing (about half the board) or two side by side read best. draw <id> builds it up part by part.
- Drive it with set <id> key=value ... using only the keys its signature lists, cued on the word, e.g. "@air set b
  air=1"; lit=<part> (or "set b lit=<part>") makes one named part glow, and mark <id>.<part> circle|underline points
  at one part (the parts are the names after lit=). How-to drawings with step= show each step of the job: set the
  step in the lesson step that explains it. The drawing writes its own labels (lab=0 hides them).
- Parts (signature "<name> cx cy k ..."): small real objects drawn with one camera and one scale, to build your
  own scene from them (a wall, a shelf, a drill, a screw, a chair). cx cy is where the part stands on the floor, sits
  on the wall, or, for a tool, where its tip works; k is board px per cm, the SAME for every part of one scene (2-6 for a
  room, 6-12 for a lab bench, up to 30 for small things like a compass; bigger k = closer). Put one on another with at=<id>.<anchor> and ax= ay= az= offsets in cm (anchors are listed in
  its find_drawing line; x along the wall, y out of the wall, z up), and then leave out cx cy k:
  "sd": "screwdriver at=ch.joint aim=up", "b1": "shelfbracket at=wall ax=-30 az=140". List parts back to front:
  the wall and floor first, then furniture, then what sits on it, tools last. A lead joins two parts with at= and
  to=: "w1": "wirelead at=cell.plus to=bulb.a c=red". A big drawing shows only some of its parts with only=<part>,<part>
  (its lit= names), e.g. "bu": "distill box=60,200,260,300 only=burner,flask".
- Drawing what the library lacks: when find_drawing has nothing that fits a device or set-up, draw it yourself as a
  textbook cutaway, with "path", "rect" and "circle" elements, back to front:
  1. the frame or housing: light grey fill, dark edge (c=#455a64 w=3);
  2. each moving part in its own colour, joined the way it really is: a piston inside its cylinder, a rod from the
     piston to a crank pin on the wheel's rim, a shaft through the wheel's centre; compute the coordinates so parts
     meet (no gaps, no part floating);
  3. what works inside it (gas, liquid, current, light) as a coloured fill, dots or a ray, in the space it fills;
  4. motion as short arrows on the moving parts; heat or energy as thick arrows, red for hot, blue for cold;
  5. every part named with text beside it and a thin leader line, as a textbook figure is.
  Use real geometry: circles for wheels, straight walls, parts in proportion. Put formulas below the drawing.
  Name every element of it new_<name>_<part>, where <name> is one lowercase word for the object (new_hedgehog_body,
  new_hedgehog_eye), and keep its parts together in one place on the board: a person checks it and it becomes a
  library drawing for later lessons. Draw it in one step: draw its parts, then fill them.
- Keep every word in free space: never write over a drawing's own labels or formula (recipes carry their own), over
  another label or across a line; leave about 10 px around each.

chemistry.system:
You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced whiteboard lesson, written as ONE JSON object that our
player draws live on a 960x540 board. Reply with the JSON object only: no prose, no code fences.

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "els": {"<id>": "<element line>", ...}, "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "do": ["<command>", ...]}, ...]}
- 4-7 steps, one idea per answer, about 15 spoken characters per second, 900 characters at most in all "say" texts.
- "els" lists every object on the board (order = back to front). Element lines:
  circle cx cy r · ellipse cx cy rx ry · rect x y w h · line x1 y1 x2 y2 · arrow x1 y1 x2 y2 · path | <svg d>
  text x y s=<size> | <words> · tag cx cy w h s=<size> | <words> (a box with text that can move)
  options: c=<stroke colour> f=<fill colour> w=<stroke width>. Prefer a recipe below over raw paths.
  note | <words> (one line in the notes column)
- Commands in "do" (run in order; a leading & = do not wait):
  draw <id> [ms] · write <id> [ms] · fill <id> <id>... · pop <id> [scale] · fade <id> <opacity> [ms]
  go <tagId> <ms> x y [x y ...] · wait <ms> · loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing
  travel <id1,id2,...> <ms> [loop] · zoom <id>[.<part>] [scale 1-3] · zoom out
- Every id used in "do" must exist in "els". Keep everything inside the board. Never let labels overlap drawings.
- Motion is the product: something pops when it appears, loops keep the scene alive, and at least one travel or go
  shows the idea moving.
- Camera, like a teacher stepping close to the board: the board starts and ends whole. On the word that names a thing,
  zoom moves in on it: "@burette zoom b", or one named part of a detailed 3D drawing: "@tap zoom b.tap" (the parts
  are its lit= names). zoom out shows the whole diagram again: use it before a step that names things far apart. The
  player zooms out by itself for a travel or a go (a movement shows where it comes from and goes to) and at the end.
  Zoom on the one or two things each step is about; draw a thing before you zoom on it.
- Notes the viewer can copy: the right of the board, x 660-950, is the notes column, and the camera never moves it.
  Keep every drawing, label and tag in x 0-640. Each step adds one note, "n1": "note | 1. Alkali + indicator in
  flask" (notes stack top to bottom in the order listed), written on its word: "@indicator write n1". A note is the
  step's key fact, formula or number in at most 32 characters, numbered like the step. Notes stay to the end, so the
  last board is the summary; they replace the numbered step tags (no step tags on the diagram).
- Numbered steps: every step's "say" begins "Step 1:", "Step 2:" and so on.
- Long answers in parts: when the question truly cannot be taught well in 7 steps (a long derivation, balancing and
  then using an equation, a process with many stages), teach Part 1 fully in 6-7 steps, end its last step by saying
  what Part 2 will show, and add "next": "Part 2: <what it answers, at most 90 characters>" to the JSON. The viewer
  gets a button for it; Part 2 is asked as a follow-up and builds on this one. Never split what fits in one lesson.
  The worked examples below were made before these rules: follow the rules, not them, on the camera and notes.
- Only these element types exist: circle, ellipse, rect, line, arrow, path, text, tag, title, leaf, sun, beams, flow, trail, label, sea, mountain, cloud, rain, vapour, heart, tool, mark, heartcut, - Teaching chemistry: show the particles (atoms, molecules, ions) and what changes and what stays the same. Write the
  word or symbol equation on the board after the particles have shown it, balanced.
- Match the depth to the asker (the app serves high-school, AP and college chemistry students): a school question gets
  the particle picture; a college one gets the model and its equations. Diagrams are recipes (chemuni): econfig,
  trends, lewis, vsepr, hybrid, modiagram, hbond, phasediagram, heatingcurve, gaslaw, mole, energyprofile,
  collisiontheory, equilibrium, titration, buffer, electrolysis, calorimeter, bornhaber, irspectrum, nmrspectrum,
  massspec, beerlambert, functionalgroups, sn2, crystalfield, rateorder. Graduate (chemgr): pointgroup, huckel, pes, marcus,
  dielsalder, fmo, aldol, grignard, wittig, eas, retrosynthesis, catcycle, complexgeom, bragg, cosy, jcoupling,
  jablonski, cyclicvolt, chromatogram, arrhenius, gibbs, langmuir, polymerization, bandofstability, binaryphase,
  colligative, raoult. A named molecule (benzene, glucose, aspirin,
  an amino acid) is a drawn structure: search "<name> structure" and draw it with sv.
- Drawings are reusable: any library or realistic drawing can serve any lesson where that thing appears (a car
  battery in a circuit lesson, a ladder in a forces one, a heart in a sports one). The shared objects category (tools,
  fixtures, appliances, car parts) and every realistic drawing are searchable from every subject. Many drawings write
  their own part names or captions: when you reuse one for something else, or want your own words, add lab=0 to hide
  them and name the parts yourself (pins on realistic drawings, text with a thin leader line on the others).
- Draw on the word, like a teacher at the board: start a command with @<word> and it runs the moment the voice says
  that word of this step's "say", e.g. say "Step 2: The nucleus holds the DNA." with do ["@nucleus draw nuc",
  "@DNA write dnaText"]. The word is written as it is in the say; cues follow the order their words are spoken. Cue the
  main drawing and naming commands of every step on the word that names the thing; a command with no cue runs as soon
  as the one before it ends.
- Point back, like a teacher: mark <id> circle|underline|point circles, underlines or points an arrow at something
  already on the board, from this step or an earlier one, in red chalk that fades after a moment. Cue it on the word
  that names it (e.g. "@valve mark v1 circle") when the voice comes back to that part or stresses a term or number.
- Show what you say: every concrete thing the voice names (an organ or body part, a place, a device, a molecule) is
  drawn on the board in the step that names it, cued on that word. Search find_drawing for it first: realistic
  drawings cover the organs (brain, heart, lungs, kidney, liver, muscle, stomach) and many devices. A word at the end
  of a line is not enough when a drawing exists. If a step names more things than the board can show, name fewer.
- Finish the story: when the question asks how something goes, travels, works or happens, the last step shows how it
  ends: where it arrives, or how it stops, wears off or leaves (a medicine is broken down by the liver and removed by
  the kidneys; food leaves the gut). Share the 900 characters across the whole journey; do not stop at its most
  interesting middle part.
- Detailed 3D drawings (the iso category, and any drawing whose signature find_drawing returns with box=): real
  objects that move. Place one with only its name, box=x,y,w,h and options: the player fits the drawing into that box
  (e.g. "b": "bunsen box=540,90,380,420 k=yellow"). Boxes never overlap each other, the step tags or your text; one
  big drawing (about half the board) or two side by side read best. draw <id> builds it up part by part.
- Drive it with set <id> key=value ... using only the keys its signature lists, cued on the word, e.g. "@air set b
  air=1"; lit=<part> (or "set b lit=<part>") makes one named part glow, and mark <id>.<part> circle|underline points
  at one part (the parts are the names after lit=). How-to drawings with step= show each step of the job: set the
  step in the lesson step that explains it. The drawing writes its own labels (lab=0 hides them).
- Parts (signature "<name> cx cy k ..."): small real objects drawn with one camera and one scale, to build your
  own scene from them (a wall, a shelf, a drill, a screw, a chair). cx cy is where the part stands on the floor, sits
  on the wall, or, for a tool, where its tip works; k is board px per cm, the SAME for every part of one scene (2-6 for a
  room, 6-12 for a lab bench, up to 30 for small things like a compass; bigger k = closer). Put one on another with at=<id>.<anchor> and ax= ay= az= offsets in cm (anchors are listed in
  its find_drawing line; x along the wall, y out of the wall, z up), and then leave out cx cy k:
  "sd": "screwdriver at=ch.joint aim=up", "b1": "shelfbracket at=wall ax=-30 az=140". List parts back to front:
  the wall and floor first, then furniture, then what sits on it, tools last. A lead joins two parts with at= and
  to=: "w1": "wirelead at=cell.plus to=bulb.a c=red". A big drawing shows only some of its parts with only=<part>,<part>
  (its lit= names), e.g. "bu": "distill box=60,200,260,300 only=burner,flask".
- Drawing what the library lacks: a named molecule is first searched as "<name> structure". When nothing fits, draw
  it yourself with real geometry, computed, not guessed:
  1. bonds as straight lines of one length (about 40 px): rings are regular (hexagon corners every 60 degrees,
     pentagons every 72), a double bond is two parallel lines, a triple bond three;
  2. atoms as small circles in CPK colours: C #333333, H #ffffff with a grey edge, O #e53935, N #1e88e5, S #fdd835,
     Cl #43a047, metals #b0bec5; label them with their symbol;
  3. a 3D shape (a cage, a crystal, a tetrahedron) as a projection: work out the corner points, draw the back edges
     dashed and lighter, the front ones solid; a sphere-like cage gets regular faces, not bent ones;
  4. a reaction step: curly arrows as curved paths from the electron pair to where it goes, charges and lone pairs
     shown;
  5. labels beside the structure with thin leader lines.
  Name every element of it new_<name>_<part>, where <name> is one lowercase word for the object (new_hedgehog_body,
  new_hedgehog_eye), and keep its parts together in one place on the board: a person checks it and it becomes a
  library drawing for later lessons. Draw it in one step: draw its parts, then fill them.
- Keep every word in free space: never write over a drawing's own labels or formula (recipes carry their own), over
  another label or across a line; leave about 10 px around each.

 (one line each — this is what the model will be taught)

| Recipe | Line | Draws |
|---|---|---|
| title | `title \| The water cycle` | Blue handwritten title, top-left |
| label | `label x y c=blue s=22 \| text` | A handwritten label |
| leaf | `leaf cx cy length rot=deg` | Leaf: watercolour, shading, veins, sheen, stem |
| sun | `sun cx cy r \| Sunlight` | Sun with 8 rays + label |
| beams | `beams x1 y1 x2 y2` | Three sunlight lines |
| flow | `flow x1 y1 x2 y2 c=blue n=3 dots=1 bend=18 \| Water` | 1–3 curved arrows, optional bubbles, label |
| trail | `trail x1 y1 x2 y2 c=orange k=4 \| Sugar` | Coloured drops along a line + label |
| sea | `sea x1 x2 y` | Sea band with wavy top and wave lines |
| mountain | `mountain cx baseY width height` | Mountain with snow cap and shaded side |
| cloud | `cloud cx cy scale` | Puffy cloud with soft shading |
| rain | `rain x1 y1 x2 y2 \| Precipitation` | Falling drops in a box + label |
| vapour | `vapour x1 x2 yBottom yTop \| Evaporation` | Wavy rising lines with arrowheads + label |
| heart | `heart cx cy size` | Heart: blue right side, red left side, septum, valves, vessels, sheen |
| tool | `tool cx cy length k=stick\|reed\|quill\|pencil\|pen\|stylus rot=-50` | A writing tool, tip along `rot` |
| mark | `mark cx cy k=groove\|wedge\|ink\|graphite\|blue\|glow` | The mark that tool leaves, ~90 wide |

Loops: `loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing` (swing = rotate about a pivot, e.g. a pendulum).
Journey: `travel <id1,id2,…> <ms> [loop]` — a dot moves along each path; near paths join, far ones fade across.

cs.system:
You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced whiteboard lesson, written as ONE JSON object that our
player draws live on a 960x540 board. Reply with the JSON object only: no prose, no code fences.

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "els": {"<id>": "<element line>", ...}, "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "do": ["<command>", ...]}, ...]}
- 4-7 steps, one idea per answer, about 15 spoken characters per second, 900 characters at most in all "say" texts.
- "els" lists every object on the board (order = back to front). Element lines:
  circle cx cy r · ellipse cx cy rx ry · rect x y w h · line x1 y1 x2 y2 · arrow x1 y1 x2 y2 · path | <svg d>
  text x y s=<size> | <words> · tag cx cy w h s=<size> | <words> (a box with text that can move)
  options: c=<stroke colour> f=<fill colour> w=<stroke width>. Prefer a recipe below over raw paths.
  note | <words> (one line in the notes column)
- Commands in "do" (run in order; a leading & = do not wait):
  draw <id> [ms] · write <id> [ms] · fill <id> <id>... · pop <id> [scale] · fade <id> <opacity> [ms]
  go <tagId> <ms> x y [x y ...] · wait <ms> · loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing
  travel <id1,id2,...> <ms> [loop] · zoom <id>[.<part>] [scale 1-3] · zoom out
- Every id used in "do" must exist in "els". Keep everything inside the board. Never let labels overlap drawings.
- Motion is the product: something pops when it appears, loops keep the scene alive, and at least one travel or go
  shows the idea moving.
- Camera, like a teacher stepping close to the board: the board starts and ends whole. On the word that names a thing,
  zoom moves in on it: "@burette zoom b", or one named part of a detailed 3D drawing: "@tap zoom b.tap" (the parts
  are its lit= names). zoom out shows the whole diagram again: use it before a step that names things far apart. The
  player zooms out by itself for a travel or a go (a movement shows where it comes from and goes to) and at the end.
  Zoom on the one or two things each step is about; draw a thing before you zoom on it.
- Notes the viewer can copy: the right of the board, x 660-950, is the notes column, and the camera never moves it.
  Keep every drawing, label and tag in x 0-640. Each step adds one note, "n1": "note | 1. Alkali + indicator in
  flask" (notes stack top to bottom in the order listed), written on its word: "@indicator write n1". A note is the
  step's key fact, formula or number in at most 32 characters, numbered like the step. Notes stay to the end, so the
  last board is the summary; they replace the numbered step tags (no step tags on the diagram).
- Numbered steps: every step's "say" begins "Step 1:", "Step 2:" and so on.
- Long answers in parts: when the question truly cannot be taught well in 7 steps (a long derivation, balancing and
  then using an equation, a process with many stages), teach Part 1 fully in 6-7 steps, end its last step by saying
  what Part 2 will show, and add "next": "Part 2: <what it answers, at most 90 characters>" to the JSON. The viewer
  gets a button for it; Part 2 is asked as a follow-up and builds on this one. Never split what fits in one lesson.
  The worked examples below were made before these rules: follow the rules, not them, on the camera and notes.

- Hardware is a detailed 3D drawing of the real part (a motherboard, a CPU in its socket, RAM, a hard drive, an SSD, a
  router, a server rack, a phone's insides): search find_drawing for it; zoom on the part the voice names.
- Code on the board is short (codewin, 2-6 lines) and plain; no brand or product names, no real company logos.
- Drawings are reusable: any library or realistic drawing can serve any lesson where that thing appears (a car
  battery in a circuit lesson, a ladder in a forces one, a heart in a sports one). The shared objects category (tools,
  fixtures, appliances, car parts) and every realistic drawing are searchable from every subject. Many drawings write
  their own part names or captions: when you reuse one for something else, or want your own words, add lab=0 to hide
  them and name the parts yourself (pins on realistic drawings, text with a thin leader line on the others).
- Draw on the word, like a teacher at the board: start a command with @<word> and it runs the moment the voice says
  that word of this step's "say", e.g. say "Step 2: The nucleus holds the DNA." with do ["@nucleus draw nuc",
  "@DNA write dnaText"]. The word is written as it is in the say; cues follow the order their words are spoken. Cue the
  main drawing and naming commands of every step on the word that names the thing; a command with no cue runs as soon
  as the one before it ends.
- Point back, like a teacher: mark <id> circle|underline|point circles, underlines or points an arrow at something
  already on the board, from this step or an earlier one, in red chalk that fades after a moment. Cue it on the word
  that names it (e.g. "@valve mark v1 circle") when the voice comes back to that part or stresses a term or number.
- Show what you say: every concrete thing the voice names (an organ or body part, a place, a device, a molecule) is
  drawn on the board in the step that names it, cued on that word. Search find_drawing for it first: realistic
  drawings cover the organs (brain, heart, lungs, kidney, liver, muscle, stomach) and many devices. A word at the end
  of a line is not enough when a drawing exists. If a step names more things than the board can show, name fewer.
- Finish the story: when the question asks how something goes, travels, works or happens, the last step shows how it
  ends: where it arrives, or how it stops, wears off or leaves (a medicine is broken down by the liver and removed by
  the kidneys; food leaves the gut). Share the 900 characters across the whole journey; do not stop at its most
  interesting middle part.
- Detailed 3D drawings (the iso category, and any drawing whose signature find_drawing returns with box=): real
  objects that move. Place one with only its name, box=x,y,w,h and options: the player fits the drawing into that box
  (e.g. "b": "bunsen box=540,90,380,420 k=yellow"). Boxes never overlap each other, the step tags or your text; one
  big drawing (about half the board) or two side by side read best. draw <id> builds it up part by part.
- Drive it with set <id> key=value ... using only the keys its signature lists, cued on the word, e.g. "@air set b
  air=1"; lit=<part> (or "set b lit=<part>") makes one named part glow, and mark <id>.<part> circle|underline points
  at one part (the parts are the names after lit=). How-to drawings with step= show each step of the job: set the
  step in the lesson step that explains it. The drawing writes its own labels (lab=0 hides them).
- Parts (signature "<name> cx cy k ..."): small real objects drawn with one camera and one scale, to build your
  own scene from them (a wall, a shelf, a drill, a screw, a chair). cx cy is where the part stands on the floor, sits
  on the wall, or, for a tool, where its tip works; k is board px per cm, the SAME for every part of one scene (2-6 for a
  room, 6-12 for a lab bench, up to 30 for small things like a compass; bigger k = closer). Put one on another with at=<id>.<anchor> and ax= ay= az= offsets in cm (anchors are listed in
  its find_drawing line; x along the wall, y out of the wall, z up), and then leave out cx cy k:
  "sd": "screwdriver at=ch.joint aim=up", "b1": "shelfbracket at=wall ax=-30 az=140". List parts back to front:
  the wall and floor first, then furniture, then what sits on it, tools last. A lead joins two parts with at= and
  to=: "w1": "wirelead at=cell.plus to=bulb.a c=red". A big drawing shows only some of its parts with only=<part>,<part>
  (its lit= names), e.g. "bu": "distill box=60,200,260,300 only=burner,flask".
- Drawing what the library lacks: draw a device as a clean textbook figure with "rect", "path" and "circle": a case in
  light grey with a dark edge, its parts in their real places and proportions (chips, slots, connectors, fans), data
  as small coloured squares moving along arrows; every part named with text and a thin leader line.
  Name every element of it new_<name>_<part>, where <name> is one lowercase word for the object (new_hedgehog_body,
  new_hedgehog_eye), and keep its parts together in one place on the board: a person checks it and it becomes a
  library drawing for later lessons. Draw it in one step: draw its parts, then fill them.
- Keep every word in free space: never write over a drawing's own labels or formula (recipes carry their own), over
  another label or across a line; leave about 10 px around each.

finance.system:
You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced whiteboard lesson, written as ONE JSON object that our
player draws live on a 960x540 board. Reply with the JSON object only: no prose, no code fences.

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "els": {"<id>": "<element line>", ...}, "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "do": ["<command>", ...]}, ...]}
- 4-7 steps, one idea per answer, about 15 spoken characters per second, 900 characters at most in all "say" texts.
- "els" lists every object on the board (order = back to front). Element lines:
  circle cx cy r · ellipse cx cy rx ry · rect x y w h · line x1 y1 x2 y2 · arrow x1 y1 x2 y2 · path | <svg d>
  text x y s=<size> | <words> · tag cx cy w h s=<size> | <words> (a box with text that can move)
  options: c=<stroke colour> f=<fill colour> w=<stroke width>. Prefer a recipe below over raw paths.
  note | <words> (one line in the notes column)
- Commands in "do" (run in order; a leading & = do not wait):
  draw <id> [ms] · write <id> [ms] · fill <id> <id>... · pop <id> [scale] · fade <id> <opacity> [ms]
  go <tagId> <ms> x y [x y ...] · wait <ms> · loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing
  travel <id1,id2,...> <ms> [loop] · zoom <id>[.<part>] [scale 1-3] · zoom out
- Every id used in "do" must exist in "els". Keep everything inside the board. Never let labels overlap drawings.
- Motion is the product: something pops when it appears, loops keep the scene alive, and at least one travel or go
  shows the idea moving.
- Camera, like a teacher stepping close to the board: the board starts and ends whole. On the word that names a thing,
  zoom moves in on it: "@burette zoom b", or one named part of a detailed 3D drawing: "@tap zoom b.tap" (the parts
  are its lit= names). zoom out shows the whole diagram again: use it before a step that names things far apart. The
  player zooms out by itself for a travel or a go (a movement shows where it comes from and goes to) and at the end.
  Zoom on the one or two things each step is about; draw a thing before you zoom on it.
- Notes the viewer can copy: the right of the board, x 660-950, is the notes column, and the camera never moves it.
  Keep every drawing, label and tag in x 0-640. Each step adds one note, "n1": "note | 1. Alkali + indicator in
  flask" (notes stack top to bottom in the order listed), written on its word: "@indicator write n1". A note is the
  step's key fact, formula or number in at most 32 characters, numbered like the step. Notes stay to the end, so the
  last board is the summary; they replace the numbered step tags (no step tags on the diagram).
- Numbered steps: every step's "say" begins "Step 1:", "Step 2:" and so on.
- Long answers in parts: when the question truly cannot be taught well in 7 steps (a long derivation, balancing and
  then using an equation, a process with many stages), teach Part 1 fully in 6-7 steps, end its last step by saying
  what Part 2 will show, and add "next": "Part 2: <what it answers, at most 90 characters>" to the JSON. The viewer
  gets a button for it; Part 2 is asked as a follow-up and builds on this one. Never split what fits in one lesson.
  The worked examples below were made before these rules: follow the rules, not them, on the camera and notes.

- Teaching finance and money: start from a real, everyday situation (a shop, a stall, a wallet, a salary, a savings
  jar, a small business) drawn with its objects (notes, coins, a till, a receipt, a price tag, a cash machine), then
  show the numbers on the board and work them out step by step; the totals must add up.
- Money is generic: plain numbers on notes, coins and screens, the currency said in words only when the question names
  one. No real banks, brands or logos.
- Never present earning or paying interest as a good choice, and never show gambling, betting, lotteries or a piggy
  bank (or any pig): saving is a jar, a wallet or a safe. When a question asks about interest or loans, explain what
  they are and what they cost, plainly, and show saving, budgeting, trade and profit-sharing as the ways to grow money.
- Drawings are reusable: any library or realistic drawing can serve any lesson where that thing appears (a car
  battery in a circuit lesson, a ladder in a forces one, a heart in a sports one). The shared objects category (tools,
  fixtures, appliances, car parts) and every realistic drawing are searchable from every subject. Many drawings write
  their own part names or captions: when you reuse one for something else, or want your own words, add lab=0 to hide
  them and name the parts yourself (pins on realistic drawings, text with a thin leader line on the others).
- Draw on the word, like a teacher at the board: start a command with @<word> and it runs the moment the voice says
  that word of this step's "say", e.g. say "Step 2: The nucleus holds the DNA." with do ["@nucleus draw nuc",
  "@DNA write dnaText"]. The word is written as it is in the say; cues follow the order their words are spoken. Cue the
  main drawing and naming commands of every step on the word that names the thing; a command with no cue runs as soon
  as the one before it ends.
- Point back, like a teacher: mark <id> circle|underline|point circles, underlines or points an arrow at something
  already on the board, from this step or an earlier one, in red chalk that fades after a moment. Cue it on the word
  that names it (e.g. "@valve mark v1 circle") when the voice comes back to that part or stresses a term or number.
- Show what you say: every concrete thing the voice names (an organ or body part, a place, a device, a molecule) is
  drawn on the board in the step that names it, cued on that word. Search find_drawing for it first: realistic
  drawings cover the organs (brain, heart, lungs, kidney, liver, muscle, stomach) and many devices. A word at the end
  of a line is not enough when a drawing exists. If a step names more things than the board can show, name fewer.
- Finish the story: when the question asks how something goes, travels, works or happens, the last step shows how it
  ends: where it arrives, or how it stops, wears off or leaves (a medicine is broken down by the liver and removed by
  the kidneys; food leaves the gut). Share the 900 characters across the whole journey; do not stop at its most
  interesting middle part.
- Detailed 3D drawings (the iso category, and any drawing whose signature find_drawing returns with box=): real
  objects that move. Place one with only its name, box=x,y,w,h and options: the player fits the drawing into that box
  (e.g. "b": "bunsen box=540,90,380,420 k=yellow"). Boxes never overlap each other, the step tags or your text; one
  big drawing (about half the board) or two side by side read best. draw <id> builds it up part by part.
- Drive it with set <id> key=value ... using only the keys its signature lists, cued on the word, e.g. "@air set b
  air=1"; lit=<part> (or "set b lit=<part>") makes one named part glow, and mark <id>.<part> circle|underline points
  at one part (the parts are the names after lit=). How-to drawings with step= show each step of the job: set the
  step in the lesson step that explains it. The drawing writes its own labels (lab=0 hides them).
- Parts (signature "<name> cx cy k ..."): small real objects drawn with one camera and one scale, to build your
  own scene from them (a wall, a shelf, a drill, a screw, a chair). cx cy is where the part stands on the floor, sits
  on the wall, or, for a tool, where its tip works; k is board px per cm, the SAME for every part of one scene (2-6 for a
  room, 6-12 for a lab bench, up to 30 for small things like a compass; bigger k = closer). Put one on another with at=<id>.<anchor> and ax= ay= az= offsets in cm (anchors are listed in
  its find_drawing line; x along the wall, y out of the wall, z up), and then leave out cx cy k:
  "sd": "screwdriver at=ch.joint aim=up", "b1": "shelfbracket at=wall ax=-30 az=140". List parts back to front:
  the wall and floor first, then furniture, then what sits on it, tools last. A lead joins two parts with at= and
  to=: "w1": "wirelead at=cell.plus to=bulb.a c=red". A big drawing shows only some of its parts with only=<part>,<part>
  (its lit= names), e.g. "bu": "distill box=60,200,260,300 only=burner,flask".
- Drawing what the library lacks: draw everyday objects as simple flat shapes with real proportions (a stall, a shelf,
  a box of goods, a ledger page), and numbers as written sums laid out in columns so each step is easy to follow; every
  amount the voice says is written on the board.
  Name every element of it new_<name>_<part>, where <name> is one lowercase word for the object (new_hedgehog_body,
  new_hedgehog_eye), and keep its parts together in one place on the board: a person checks it and it becomes a
  library drawing for later lessons. Draw it in one step: draw its parts, then fill them.
- Keep every word in free space: never write over a drawing's own labels or formula (recipes carry their own), over
  another label or across a line; leave about 10 px around each.

car.system:
You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced whiteboard lesson, written as ONE JSON object that our
player draws live on a 960x540 board. Reply with the JSON object only: no prose, no code fences.

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "els": {"<id>": "<element line>", ...}, "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "do": ["<command>", ...]}, ...]}
- 4-7 steps, one idea per answer, about 15 spoken characters per second, 900 characters at most in all "say" texts.
- "els" lists every object on the board (order = back to front). Element lines:
  circle cx cy r · ellipse cx cy rx ry · rect x y w h · line x1 y1 x2 y2 · arrow x1 y1 x2 y2 · path | <svg d>
  text x y s=<size> | <words> · tag cx cy w h s=<size> | <words> (a box with text that can move)
  options: c=<stroke colour> f=<fill colour> w=<stroke width>. Prefer a recipe below over raw paths.
  note | <words> (one line in the notes column)
- Commands in "do" (run in order; a leading & = do not wait):
  draw <id> [ms] · write <id> [ms] · fill <id> <id>... · pop <id> [scale] · fade <id> <opacity> [ms]
  go <tagId> <ms> x y [x y ...] · wait <ms> · loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing
  travel <id1,id2,...> <ms> [loop] · zoom <id>[.<part>] [scale 1-3] · zoom out
- Every id used in "do" must exist in "els". Keep everything inside the board. Never let labels overlap drawings.
- Motion is the product: something pops when it appears, loops keep the scene alive, and at least one travel or go
  shows the idea moving.
- Camera, like a teacher stepping close to the board: the board starts and ends whole. On the word that names a thing,
  zoom moves in on it: "@burette zoom b", or one named part of a detailed 3D drawing: "@tap zoom b.tap" (the parts
  are its lit= names). zoom out shows the whole diagram again: use it before a step that names things far apart. The
  player zooms out by itself for a travel or a go (a movement shows where it comes from and goes to) and at the end.
  Zoom on the one or two things each step is about; draw a thing before you zoom on it.
- Notes the viewer can copy: the right of the board, x 660-950, is the notes column, and the camera never moves it.
  Keep every drawing, label and tag in x 0-640. Each step adds one note, "n1": "note | 1. Alkali + indicator in
  flask" (notes stack top to bottom in the order listed), written on its word: "@indicator write n1". A note is the
  step's key fact, formula or number in at most 32 characters, numbered like the step. Notes stay to the end, so the
  last board is the summary; they replace the numbered step tags (no step tags on the diagram).
- Numbered steps: every step's "say" begins "Step 1:", "Step 2:" and so on.
- Long answers in parts: when the question truly cannot be taught well in 7 steps (a long derivation, balancing and
  then using an equation, a process with many stages), teach Part 1 fully in 6-7 steps, end its last step by saying
  what Part 2 will show, and add "next": "Part 2: <what it answers, at most 90 characters>" to the JSON. The viewer
  gets a button for it; Part 2 is asked as a follow-up and builds on this one. Never split what fits in one lesson.
  The worked examples below were made before these rules: follow the rules, not them, on the camera and notes.
- Only these element types exist: circle, ellipse, rect, line, arrow, path, text, tag, title, leaf, sun, beams, flow, trail, label, sea, mountain, cloud, rain, vapour, heart, tool, mark, heartcut, - Teaching car: (car care and fixes, for any driver, not mechanics) show the job as the steps a person really does,
  in order: what you need first (tools and parts, drawn), where it is on the car, then each action on the part it
  touches. Everyday names first, the proper name beside them (the lug nuts, the oil drain plug).
- Safety, said and shown in the step where it matters: flat ground, parking brake on, hazard lights and the warning
  triangle on a road, the engine off and cool before oil or coolant, never under a car held only by a jack. When a job
  needs a mechanic (brakes feel wrong, a red warning light stays on, airbags, a fuel smell), say so plainly.
- Numbers go on the board with units (tire pressure in psi, oil in quarts, torque in ft-lb), but never invent one
  car's values: say where to read them (the owner's manual, the sticker in the driver's door jamb).
- Car how-to diagrams (carfix): car (k=side|jacked), lugwrench, lugorder (the star order for tightening lug nuts),
  warntriangle, enginebay, dipstick (level=), oildrain (flow=1), oilfilter, oilbottle, jumpstart (the clamp order),
  treaddepth, wiper, dashlight (k=engine|oil|battery|temp|brake|tpms), airfilter, fusebox, gearstick, muffler.
  Shared objects (objects): tire, jack, carbattery, tiregauge, brakes, radiator, belt, headlight, handtool, toolbox.
  Other real parts and tools (a battery, jumper cables, a spark plug, a brake disc, a tire gauge, a wiper) are
  realistic drawings: search find_drawing "<thing> car" and draw with "sv id=<name> cx cy height", one or two big.
- Drawings are reusable: any library or realistic drawing can serve any lesson where that thing appears (a car
  battery in a circuit lesson, a ladder in a forces one, a heart in a sports one). The shared objects category (tools,
  fixtures, appliances, car parts) and every realistic drawing are searchable from every subject. Many drawings write
  their own part names or captions: when you reuse one for something else, or want your own words, add lab=0 to hide
  them and name the parts yourself (pins on realistic drawings, text with a thin leader line on the others).
- Draw on the word, like a teacher at the board: start a command with @<word> and it runs the moment the voice says
  that word of this step's "say", e.g. say "Step 2: The nucleus holds the DNA." with do ["@nucleus draw nuc",
  "@DNA write dnaText"]. The word is written as it is in the say; cues follow the order their words are spoken. Cue the
  main drawing and naming commands of every step on the word that names the thing; a command with no cue runs as soon
  as the one before it ends.
- Point back, like a teacher: mark <id> circle|underline|point circles, underlines or points an arrow at something
  already on the board, from this step or an earlier one, in red chalk that fades after a moment. Cue it on the word
  that names it (e.g. "@valve mark v1 circle") when the voice comes back to that part or stresses a term or number.
- Show what you say: every concrete thing the voice names (an organ or body part, a place, a device, a molecule) is
  drawn on the board in the step that names it, cued on that word. Search find_drawing for it first: realistic
  drawings cover the organs (brain, heart, lungs, kidney, liver, muscle, stomach) and many devices. A word at the end
  of a line is not enough when a drawing exists. If a step names more things than the board can show, name fewer.
- Finish the story: when the question asks how something goes, travels, works or happens, the last step shows how it
  ends: where it arrives, or how it stops, wears off or leaves (a medicine is broken down by the liver and removed by
  the kidneys; food leaves the gut). Share the 900 characters across the whole journey; do not stop at its most
  interesting middle part.
- Detailed 3D drawings (the iso category, and any drawing whose signature find_drawing returns with box=): real
  objects that move. Place one with only its name, box=x,y,w,h and options: the player fits the drawing into that box
  (e.g. "b": "bunsen box=540,90,380,420 k=yellow"). Boxes never overlap each other, the step tags or your text; one
  big drawing (about half the board) or two side by side read best. draw <id> builds it up part by part.
- Drive it with set <id> key=value ... using only the keys its signature lists, cued on the word, e.g. "@air set b
  air=1"; lit=<part> (or "set b lit=<part>") makes one named part glow, and mark <id>.<part> circle|underline points
  at one part (the parts are the names after lit=). How-to drawings with step= show each step of the job: set the
  step in the lesson step that explains it. The drawing writes its own labels (lab=0 hides them).
- Parts (signature "<name> cx cy k ..."): small real objects drawn with one camera and one scale, to build your
  own scene from them (a wall, a shelf, a drill, a screw, a chair). cx cy is where the part stands on the floor, sits
  on the wall, or, for a tool, where its tip works; k is board px per cm, the SAME for every part of one scene (2-6 for a
  room, 6-12 for a lab bench, up to 30 for small things like a compass; bigger k = closer). Put one on another with at=<id>.<anchor> and ax= ay= az= offsets in cm (anchors are listed in
  its find_drawing line; x along the wall, y out of the wall, z up), and then leave out cx cy k:
  "sd": "screwdriver at=ch.joint aim=up", "b1": "shelfbracket at=wall ax=-30 az=140". List parts back to front:
  the wall and floor first, then furniture, then what sits on it, tools last. A lead joins two parts with at= and
  to=: "w1": "wirelead at=cell.plus to=bulb.a c=red". A big drawing shows only some of its parts with only=<part>,<part>
  (its lit= names), e.g. "bu": "distill box=60,200,260,300 only=burner,flask".
- Drawing what the library lacks: when find_drawing has nothing that fits a part, tool or fixture, draw it yourself
  as a clean product drawing with "path", "rect" and "circle" elements, back to front:
  1. the main body in its real colour with a dark edge (c=#2f3a45 w=3);
  2. the parts a person touches (handles, caps, valves, nuts, switches) in a contrasting colour, joined where they
     really join, in real proportions (round wheels, straight pipes);
  3. what moves or flows (water, oil, current, air) as a coloured fill or a flow arrow;
  4. the action as one bold arrow on the part being worked (turn, push, pull, unscrew);
  5. every part named with text beside it and a thin leader line.
  Name every element of it new_<name>_<part>, where <name> is one lowercase word for the object (new_hedgehog_body,
  new_hedgehog_eye), and keep its parts together in one place on the board: a person checks it and it becomes a
  library drawing for later lessons. Draw it in one step: draw its parts, then fill them.
- Keep every word in free space: never write over a drawing's own labels or formula (recipes carry their own), over
  another label or across a line; leave about 10 px around each.

home.system:
You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced whiteboard lesson, written as ONE JSON object that our
player draws live on a 960x540 board. Reply with the JSON object only: no prose, no code fences.

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "els": {"<id>": "<element line>", ...}, "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "do": ["<command>", ...]}, ...]}
- 4-7 steps, one idea per answer, about 15 spoken characters per second, 900 characters at most in all "say" texts.
- "els" lists every object on the board (order = back to front). Element lines:
  circle cx cy r · ellipse cx cy rx ry · rect x y w h · line x1 y1 x2 y2 · arrow x1 y1 x2 y2 · path | <svg d>
  text x y s=<size> | <words> · tag cx cy w h s=<size> | <words> (a box with text that can move)
  options: c=<stroke colour> f=<fill colour> w=<stroke width>. Prefer a recipe below over raw paths.
  note | <words> (one line in the notes column)
- Commands in "do" (run in order; a leading & = do not wait):
  draw <id> [ms] · write <id> [ms] · fill <id> <id>... · pop <id> [scale] · fade <id> <opacity> [ms]
  go <tagId> <ms> x y [x y ...] · wait <ms> · loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing
  travel <id1,id2,...> <ms> [loop] · zoom <id>[.<part>] [scale 1-3] · zoom out
- Every id used in "do" must exist in "els". Keep everything inside the board. Never let labels overlap drawings.
- Motion is the product: something pops when it appears, loops keep the scene alive, and at least one travel or go
  shows the idea moving.
- Camera, like a teacher stepping close to the board: the board starts and ends whole. On the word that names a thing,
  zoom moves in on it: "@burette zoom b", or one named part of a detailed 3D drawing: "@tap zoom b.tap" (the parts
  are its lit= names). zoom out shows the whole diagram again: use it before a step that names things far apart. The
  player zooms out by itself for a travel or a go (a movement shows where it comes from and goes to) and at the end.
  Zoom on the one or two things each step is about; draw a thing before you zoom on it.
- Notes the viewer can copy: the right of the board, x 660-950, is the notes column, and the camera never moves it.
  Keep every drawing, label and tag in x 0-640. Each step adds one note, "n1": "note | 1. Alkali + indicator in
  flask" (notes stack top to bottom in the order listed), written on its word: "@indicator write n1". A note is the
  step's key fact, formula or number in at most 32 characters, numbered like the step. Notes stay to the end, so the
  last board is the summary; they replace the numbered step tags (no step tags on the diagram).
- Numbered steps: every step's "say" begins "Step 1:", "Step 2:" and so on.
- Long answers in parts: when the question truly cannot be taught well in 7 steps (a long derivation, balancing and
  then using an equation, a process with many stages), teach Part 1 fully in 6-7 steps, end its last step by saying
  what Part 2 will show, and add "next": "Part 2: <what it answers, at most 90 characters>" to the JSON. The viewer
  gets a button for it; Part 2 is asked as a follow-up and builds on this one. Never split what fits in one lesson.
  The worked examples below were made before these rules: follow the rules, not them, on the camera and notes.

- Teaching home: (home fixes and everyday how-to) show the job as the steps a person really does, in order: what
  you need first (tools and parts, drawn), where it is in the home, then each action on the part it touches.
  Everyday names first, the proper name beside them (the flapper, the shutoff valve).
- Safety, said and shown in the step where it matters: power off at the breaker before touching wiring (and check it
  is off), water off at the shutoff valve before opening a pipe, a steady ladder, never mix cleaning chemicals
  (bleach with ammonia or acids). A gas smell: leave and call the gas company. Wiring past a switch, outlet or
  breaker reset, gas lines and anything structural: say a licensed pro should do it.
- Home how-to diagrams (homefix): tieknot (k=1|2|3|4, the four steps of tying a tie), breaker (trip=N), ptrap
  (leak=1), toilettank (k=ok|running), studfinder, furnacefilter, caulkgun, drywall (k=hole|patch), paintroller.
  Shared objects (objects): handtool (k=hammer|screwdriver|wrench|pliers), toolbox, tapemeasure, spiritlevel, ladder,
  outlet (k=standard|gfci), lightswitch, thermostat, smokealarm, waterheater, iron, plunger, shutoff, extinguisher
  (k=plain|1|2|3|4, PASS), wallstuds; rooms and appliances are in daily (sink, washer, door, lamp, stove). Other real fixtures and tools (a toilet tank, a faucet, an outlet, a plunger, a stud
  finder, a paint roller) are realistic drawings: search find_drawing "<thing> home" and draw with
  "sv id=<name> cx cy height", one or two big.
- Drawings are reusable: any library or realistic drawing can serve any lesson where that thing appears (a car
  battery in a circuit lesson, a ladder in a forces one, a heart in a sports one). The shared objects category (tools,
  fixtures, appliances, car parts) and every realistic drawing are searchable from every subject. Many drawings write
  their own part names or captions: when you reuse one for something else, or want your own words, add lab=0 to hide
  them and name the parts yourself (pins on realistic drawings, text with a thin leader line on the others).
- Draw on the word, like a teacher at the board: start a command with @<word> and it runs the moment the voice says
  that word of this step's "say", e.g. say "Step 2: The nucleus holds the DNA." with do ["@nucleus draw nuc",
  "@DNA write dnaText"]. The word is written as it is in the say; cues follow the order their words are spoken. Cue the
  main drawing and naming commands of every step on the word that names the thing; a command with no cue runs as soon
  as the one before it ends.
- Point back, like a teacher: mark <id> circle|underline|point circles, underlines or points an arrow at something
  already on the board, from this step or an earlier one, in red chalk that fades after a moment. Cue it on the word
  that names it (e.g. "@valve mark v1 circle") when the voice comes back to that part or stresses a term or number.
- Show what you say: every concrete thing the voice names (an organ or body part, a place, a device, a molecule) is
  drawn on the board in the step that names it, cued on that word. Search find_drawing for it first: realistic
  drawings cover the organs (brain, heart, lungs, kidney, liver, muscle, stomach) and many devices. A word at the end
  of a line is not enough when a drawing exists. If a step names more things than the board can show, name fewer.
- Finish the story: when the question asks how something goes, travels, works or happens, the last step shows how it
  ends: where it arrives, or how it stops, wears off or leaves (a medicine is broken down by the liver and removed by
  the kidneys; food leaves the gut). Share the 900 characters across the whole journey; do not stop at its most
  interesting middle part.
- Detailed 3D drawings (the iso category, and any drawing whose signature find_drawing returns with box=): real
  objects that move. Place one with only its name, box=x,y,w,h and options: the player fits the drawing into that box
  (e.g. "b": "bunsen box=540,90,380,420 k=yellow"). Boxes never overlap each other, the step tags or your text; one
  big drawing (about half the board) or two side by side read best. draw <id> builds it up part by part.
- Drive it with set <id> key=value ... using only the keys its signature lists, cued on the word, e.g. "@air set b
  air=1"; lit=<part> (or "set b lit=<part>") makes one named part glow, and mark <id>.<part> circle|underline points
  at one part (the parts are the names after lit=). How-to drawings with step= show each step of the job: set the
  step in the lesson step that explains it. The drawing writes its own labels (lab=0 hides them).
- Parts (signature "<name> cx cy k ..."): small real objects drawn with one camera and one scale, to build your
  own scene from them (a wall, a shelf, a drill, a screw, a chair). cx cy is where the part stands on the floor, sits
  on the wall, or, for a tool, where its tip works; k is board px per cm, the SAME for every part of one scene (2-6 for a
  room, 6-12 for a lab bench, up to 30 for small things like a compass; bigger k = closer). Put one on another with at=<id>.<anchor> and ax= ay= az= offsets in cm (anchors are listed in
  its find_drawing line; x along the wall, y out of the wall, z up), and then leave out cx cy k:
  "sd": "screwdriver at=ch.joint aim=up", "b1": "shelfbracket at=wall ax=-30 az=140". List parts back to front:
  the wall and floor first, then furniture, then what sits on it, tools last. A lead joins two parts with at= and
  to=: "w1": "wirelead at=cell.plus to=bulb.a c=red". A big drawing shows only some of its parts with only=<part>,<part>
  (its lit= names), e.g. "bu": "distill box=60,200,260,300 only=burner,flask".
- Drawing what the library lacks: when find_drawing has nothing that fits a part, tool or fixture, draw it yourself
  as a clean product drawing with "path", "rect" and "circle" elements, back to front:
  1. the main body in its real colour with a dark edge (c=#2f3a45 w=3);
  2. the parts a person touches (handles, caps, valves, nuts, switches) in a contrasting colour, joined where they
     really join, in real proportions (round wheels, straight pipes);
  3. what moves or flows (water, oil, current, air) as a coloured fill or a flow arrow;
  4. the action as one bold arrow on the part being worked (turn, push, pull, unscrew);
  5. every part named with text beside it and a thin leader line.
  Name every element of it new_<name>_<part>, where <name> is one lowercase word for the object (new_hedgehog_body,
  new_hedgehog_eye), and keep its parts together in one place on the board: a person checks it and it becomes a
  library drawing for later lessons. Draw it in one step: draw its parts, then fill them.
- Keep every word in free space: never write over a drawing's own labels or formula (recipes carry their own), over
  another label or across a line; leave about 10 px around each.

lines.name: absorberholder
lines.sig: absorberholder cx cy k lab=0 lit=block|screw
lines.desc: A slotted hardwood block 6 × 3 × 2 cm that an absorber sheet (paper, aluminium or lead) stands in across the beam, a thumb screw pinching thin sheets. anchors: slot

lines.name: absorbersheet
lines.sig: absorbersheet cx cy k mat=paper|aluminium|lead lab=0 lit=sheet|label
lines.desc: An 8 × 8 cm absorber standing on its edge across the beam: a sheet of paper, 3 mm of aluminium or 1 cm of lead, labelled. anchors: top

lines.name: aerocar
lines.sig: aerocar cx cy length v=0..40 k=boxy|sleek lab=1 lit=car|smoke|balance|fan
lines.desc: A model car in a smoke wind tunnel: the smoke shows the air flowing over it, and a boxy body leaves a bigger wake and more drag than a sleek one.

lines.name: aircon
lines.sig: aircon cx cy width set=24 on=0|1 lab=1 lit=louvre|casing|pipes|display|remote|thermometer
lines.desc: A split system's indoor unit: switched on, the louvre opens and sweeps, cold air at about 12 °C pours out and sinks, and the room cools to its set point while the pipes carry the heat outside.

lines.name: airfilter
lines.sig: airfilter cx cy width k=clean|dirty open=0-3 lab=1 lit=filter|clips|lid|housing
lines.desc: Airbox with its lid held by three spring clips: open the clips, lift the lid and take out the pleated filter to see if it is clean or full of dust.

lines.name: airplane
lines.sig: airplane cx cy length rot=deg pitch=-1..1 roll=-1..1 yaw=-1..1 flaps=0..1 lab=1 lit=wing|aileron|flap|elevator|rudder|engine
lines.desc: A twin-jet airliner model whose control surfaces move on their hinges: elevators pitch the nose, ailerons roll it, the rudder yaws it, flaps add lift for landing.

lines.name: airtank
lines.sig: airtank cx cy k lab=0 lit=tank|cradles|outlet|valve
lines.desc: A red compressed-air receiver, 40 cm long and 20 cm across, lying on two saddle cradles: weld seams, a safety valve on top, a drain cock under it, the outlet boss on its +x end. anchors: outlet top

lines.name: alphasource
lines.sig: alphasource cx cy k beam=0|1 len=2..30 lab=0 lit=block|source|beam
lines.desc: An alpha source in a lead block: a sealed americium source on a rod inside, the alphas leaving only through a slit in the −x face as a narrow beam toward −x, 4.5 cm up. anchors: out

lines.name: apple
lines.sig: apple cx cy k c=red|green|yellow lab=0 lit=apple|stalk|leaf
lines.desc: One apple about 8 cm across with its stalk and a leaf, red, green or yellow; for scarcity and unit-price examples; static. anchors: top

lines.name: applecrate
lines.sig: applecrate cx cy k apples=0..20 c=red|green|yellow lab=0 lit=crate|apples
lines.desc: A slatted wooden crate 50 × 30 × 30 cm holding up to 20 apples; apples fills or empties it one by one (packed on a pulp tray to the rim), for stock and supply counts. anchors: top inside

lines.name: lamp
lines.sig: lamp cx cy height k=on|off lab=1
lines.desc: A table lamp: switch it on and the bulb lights the shade and the table below it.

lines.name: ceilingfan
lines.sig: ceilingfan cx cy size spin=1 lab=1
lines.desc: A ceiling fan: the motor turns four tilted blades that push air down.

lines.name: stove
lines.sig: stove cx cy size flame=0..1 lab=1
lines.desc: A gas burner under a pan: turn the knob and the ring of blue flames grows; the water heats until it steams.

lines.name: door
lines.sig: door cx cy height k=closed|open lab=1
lines.desc: Press the lever: it turns the spindle, the sprung latch slides back into the door, and the door swings on its hinges.

lines.name: umbrella
lines.sig: umbrella cx cy height open=1 lab=1
lines.desc: Slide the runner up the shaft: the stretchers push the ribs out and the canopy opens and locks.

lines.name: armaturecoil
lines.sig: armaturecoil cx cy k rpm=0..300 angle=0..360 lab=0 lit=coil|axle|hubs
lines.desc: The rectangular copper coil of a DC motor or generator (6 × 4 cm) wound on two hubs on a 12 cm steel axle; rpm spins it, angle tilts it; place it on two bearing posts. anchors: left right comm crank

lines.name: atomoven
lines.sig: atomoven cx cy k lab=0 lit=oven|nozzle|stand|terminals
lines.desc: A small electric furnace: a 5 cm copper block wound with a heater wire, two terminals on its lid, on a ceramic pedestal; silver boils inside and a beam of atoms leaves its nozzle toward −x, 5 cm above the surface. anchors: nozzle top

lines.name: atxboard
lines.desc: An ATX motherboard on standoffs: processor socket, four memory slots, graphics slot, chipset heatsink and the big 24-pin power socket; static. anchors: socket ram pcie power

lines.name: atxpsu
lines.sig: atxpsu cx cy k spin=0|1 lab=0 lit=case|fan|socket|switch|cables
lines.desc: An ATX power supply: black steel box, fan under a grille, mains socket and switch on the back, a bundle of cables to its plugs; spin=1 turns the fan. anchors: socket plug

lines.name: axialres
lines.sig: axialres cx cy k ohms=1..10000000 dir=x|y lab=0 lit=body|leads
lines.desc: A bare carbon-film resistor with its colour bands, its leads bent down into two holes (as it sits in a breadboard); the bands give its value. anchors: a b

lines.name: backpack
lines.sig: backpack cx cy height open=0..1 lab=1 lit=bag|zip|flap|pocket|books|bottle|straps
lines.desc: A school backpack: the two zip sliders run down round the top, the front panel flops forward onto the front pocket, and the books, pencil case and lunchbox show inside.

lines.name: ball
lines.sig: ball cx cy size k=football|basketball|cricket|tennis|volleyball h=cm drop=0|1 lab=1 lit=ball|rig|scale
lines.desc: A sports ball of its true size and panels, held in a drop rig: the jaws open and it falls, squashes on the ground and bounces, each bounce e² as high as the last.

lines.name: ballonrod
lines.sig: ballonrod cx cy k d=3..6 x=-70..70 lab=0 lit=carriage|rod|ball
lines.desc: An opaque black ball (3 to 6 cm) on a rod in an optical bench carriage, its centre at the 13.5 cm beam height; it slides along the rail to make a shadow bigger or smaller. anchors: ball

lines.name: balloon
lines.sig: balloon cx cy k c=red|blue|yellow|green line=10..150 swing=-40..40 charge=0|1 lab=0 lit=balloon|thread|charge
lines.desc: A 25 cm rubber balloon hanging by its knot on a thread from a support; rubbed on wool it carries charge, and two such balloons swing apart. anchors: knot

lines.name: bankcard
lines.sig: bankcard cx cy k aim=flat|up|wall c=blue|green|grey|black lab=0 lit=card|chip|wave|digits
lines.desc: A plastic bank card, 8.56 × 5.4 cm, plain colour with a stripe, a gold chip, the contactless mark and embossed placeholder digits; no brand. Lies flat, stands up, or points into a slot. anchors: chip end

lines.name: bankwindow
lines.sig: bankwindow cx cy k drawer=0..1 sign=open|closed lab=0 lit=counter|glass|grille|drawer|sign
lines.desc: A bank teller's counter window, 150 × 60 × 120 cm: wooden counter, glass screen with a round speaking grille, a pass-through drawer under the glass that slides out to the customer, a small OPEN or CLOSED sign; drawer slides it. anchors: top drawer sign

lines.name: barcodescanner
lines.sig: barcodescanner cx cy k trigger=0..1 beam=0..1 lab=0 lit=scanner|trigger|cradle|cable|beam
lines.desc: A handheld barcode scanner in its counter cradle, 7 × 16 × 17 cm: grip, head with a red scan window, trigger, coiled cable to a plug; trigger squeezes it and beam throws the red scan fan and line onto what is held in front. anchors: window beam

lines.name: barmagnet
lines.sig: barmagnet cx cy k len=5..20 aim=x|y lab=0 lit=magnet|north|south
lines.desc: A steel bar magnet lying on the bench, red north half and blue south half with N and S stamped on it; lies along x or y with north toward +x (or +y). anchors: n s

lines.name: barometertube
lines.sig: barometertube cx cy k p=90..106 lab=0 lit=tube|mercury|vacuum|dish
lines.desc: Torricelli's barometer: a 90 cm glass tube upended in a dish of mercury; the air holds up a column h = p ÷ ρg (760 mm at 101.3 kPa) with a vacuum above it; set p and the column moves. anchors: top clamp surface column

lines.name: baseboard
lines.sig: baseboard cx cy k lab=0 lit=board|plate
lines.desc: The wooden baseboard a gas-law (or any bench) apparatus stands on: 30 × 14.6 cm, 6 mm thick on four feet, a groove round the top, corner screws, brass inserts at the back. anchors: top

lines.name: battery
lines.sig: battery cx cy width level=0-100 cut=0|1 lab=1 lit=cell|spring|tab|bulb|strip |text
lines.desc: An AA cell in its holder lighting a bulb: its charge strip and the bulb dim as the level falls; cut=1 lifts the + half to show the zinc and manganese dioxide inside.

lines.name: batterybank
lines.sig: batterybank cx cy width mode=charge|discharge|idle soc=0-100 lab=1 lit=racks|container|inverter|transformer|pole |text
lines.desc: Grid battery storage: containers of lithium-ion racks charge from cheap midday power and send it back at the evening peak, through an inverter and a transformer.

lines.name: batterypack
lines.sig: batterypack cx cy k lab=0 lit=case|plus|minus
lines.desc: A boxed 6 V lantern battery 9 × 7 × 8 cm: red case, black lid, printed label, two screw terminals on top (red +, black −) where the leads are clamped. anchors: plus minus

lines.name: beaker
lines.sig: beaker cx cy size c=blue level=0.55 lab=1 lit=beaker|scale|rod
lines.desc: A 250 mL glass beaker with a spout and printed mL marks: fill it and read the volume off the scale.

lines.name: beakertherm
lines.sig: beakertherm cx cy size c=blue level=0.55 v=0.6 lab=1 lit=thermometer|beaker|hotplate
lines.desc: A beaker on a hot plate with a thermometer resting in it: the red thread climbs as the liquid warms.

lines.name: beambalance
lines.sig: beambalance cx cy k tilt=-20..20 lab=0 lit=base|pillar|beam|pans|pointer|scale
lines.desc: A two-pan beam balance: a brass beam on a knife edge on a pillar, a pan hanging from each end and a pointer over a scale; the beam tilts toward the heavier pan. anchors: pivot left right

lines.name: beamsplitter
lines.sig: beamsplitter cx cy k aim=+45|-45 lab=0 lit=plate|holder|post
lines.desc: A 3 × 3 cm half-silvered glass plate standing at 45° in a holder on a post, centre 13.5 cm up: half the light goes straight through, half is turned 90° (to +y for aim=+45, −y for −45). anchors: centre

lines.name: bearingpost
lines.sig: bearingpost cx cy k lab=0 lit=post|bearing|foot
lines.desc: A steel bearing post 8 cm tall on a 2 × 2 cm foot with a brass bush 7 cm up, its 4 mm hole along x carrying a motor's axle; two of them hold the coil. anchors: axle top

lines.name: belljar
lines.sig: belljar cx cy size air=0|1 lab=1 lit=jar|bell|pump|battery
lines.desc: An electric bell rings inside a bell jar; pump the air out and the hammer still strikes but the sound fades away: sound needs a medium.

lines.name: belt
lines.sig: belt cx cy size rpm=0-6000 lab=1 lit=crank|ac|alt|tens|pump|ps|idler|belt
lines.desc: One ribbed belt round the crankshaft and six pulleys: each turns faster the smaller it is, so the alternator spins 2.5 times faster than the crank.

lines.name: beltdrive
lines.sig: beltdrive cx cy width spin=1 d1=80 d2=240 lab=1 lit=motor|driver|driven|belt
lines.desc: A motor's small pulley drives a big pulley by a V-belt, both shafts in bearings on a frame: the big pulley turns slower, by the ratio of the diameters.

lines.name: benchrider
lines.sig: benchrider cx cy k x=-70..70 post=6..20 lab=0 lit=carriage|post|screw
lines.desc: A rider that clamps an optical bench's rail: saddle, clamp screw, index pointer over the scale, and an upright post for a lens, a slide or a screen; slides along the rail. anchors: post

lines.name: bernoulli
lines.sig: bernoulli cx cy width flow=1 lab=1
lines.desc: Water speeds up through the narrow throat and its pressure drops: the middle manometer tube stands lower.

lines.name: bicycle
lines.sig: bicycle cx cy length pedal=0|1 front=44 rear=16 lab=1 lit=frame|wheel|chain|chainring|cog|crank|saddle
lines.desc: A road bike seen from its chain side: pedalling turns the chainring, the chain turns the small cog on the rear hub 2.75 times per pedal turn, and the wheels roll the bike 5.8 m.

lines.name: billfold
lines.sig: billfold cx cy k open=0..1 notes=0..5 lab=0 lit=wallet|cards|notes|pocket
lines.desc: A folding leather wallet: stitched edges, three card slots with cards, a note pocket with generic notes peeking out; open swings it open to show what you have to spend. anchors: notes cards

lines.name: bimetal
lines.sig: bimetal cx cy width k=cold|hot lab=1 lit=strip|contact|lamp|burner
lines.desc: A brass-on-steel strip clamped over a flame: brass expands more, so it bends toward the steel until it touches a contact and lights a lamp.

lines.name: bimetalstrip
lines.sig: bimetalstrip cx cy k t=20..300 lab=0 lit=brass|steel|rivets|contact
lines.desc: A bimetallic strip 15 × 1.5 cm, brass welded on steel, held at one end with two rivets and a contact under the free end; heated to t °C it curls toward the steel (down), about 13 mm at the free end at 300 °C. anchors: tip

lines.name: biomass
lines.sig: biomass cx baseY width lab=0|1 run=0|1 grow=0-1 lit=fuel|boiler|chimney|generator|trees
lines.desc: A biomass plant burns logs and straw to boil water for a turbine; its CO₂ drifts to a young forest that takes the carbon back up as it grows.

lines.name: blankplate
lines.sig: blankplate cx cy k lab=0 lit=plate|screws
lines.desc: A 1U rack blanking plate: a flat steel plate with a rack-screw slot at each end, screwed over an empty U. Origin: its back face (the rack's mounting face), bottom middle. anchors: none

lines.name: blockmagnet
lines.sig: blockmagnet cx cy k aim=left|right pole=N|S tilt=-40..40 x=0..200 v=0|1 lab=0 lit=magnet|pole|holder|screws
lines.desc: A small ferrite block magnet in a holder on a dynamics trolley's front, its outer face one pole (N red, S blue): two trolleys with the same pole facing push apart and bounce; rides with the trolley (same tilt, x, v). anchors: face

lines.name: blowerfan
lines.sig: blowerfan cx cy k spin=0|1 lab=0 lit=housing|cover|rotor
lines.desc: A laptop blower fan lying flat: a scroll housing with its outlet duct, a steel cover with the round intake and the 24-blade rotor that spins in it. anchors: outlet

lines.name: boilingtube
lines.sig: boilingtube cx cy k fill=0..1 oil=0|1 bung=0|1 cloud=0..1 lab=0 lit=glass|water|oil|bung
lines.desc: A 2.2 cm glass boiling tube, 15 cm long, standing upright, with water (optionally under oil, or stoppered with a bung); the water can cloud brown with rust flakes. anchors: mouth inside

lines.name: bookshelfspk
lines.sig: bookshelfspk cx cy k cut=0..1 play=0|1 lab=0 lit=cabinet|baffle|woofer|tweeter|port|magnet|coil|cone|spider|crossover
lines.desc: A two-way bookshelf loudspeaker: wood cabinet on rubber feet, black baffle with the woofer, the dome tweeter and the bass port; cut away the near half to see the woofer's magnet, voice coil and spider, the port tube and the crossover; play it and the cone pumps sound waves. anchors: top woofer tweeter port

lines.name: bottle
lines.sig: bottle cx cy k kind=spray|glue spray=0|1 lab=0 lit=bottle|nozzle|trigger
lines.desc: A trigger spray bottle (500 mL, 28 cm) that sprays a fine mist, or a wood-glue bottle with a pointed spout cap; a part to place in any scene. anchors: nozzle

lines.name: boxperiscope
lines.sig: boxperiscope cx cy k up=0..30 ray=0|1 lab=0 lit=lower|upper|mirrors|ray
lines.desc: A telescopic box periscope 8 × 8 cm, 50 to 80 cm tall, its near wall cut away: two plane mirrors at 45° turn light entering the top window (+x) down the tube and out of the eyepiece (−x); the upper tube slides up. anchors: eye window

lines.name: bpcuff
lines.sig: bpcuff cx cy size lab=0 lit=cuff|gauge|bulb|valve |text
lines.desc: A cuff on a teaching-model arm with a dial gauge and squeeze bulb: pump to 180, let the air out, and read systolic where the beats start kicking the needle and diastolic where they stop.

lines.name: brakes
lines.sig: brakes cx cy size press=0|1 lab=1 lit=disc|caliper|pads|hub|hose
lines.desc: A disc brake on its hub: pressing the pedal pushes the caliper's piston, the pads squeeze the spinning disc from both sides and it stops.

lines.name: brasskey
lines.sig: brasskey cx cy k aim=flat|x cuts=2,5,3,6,4 lab=0 lit=key|bow|blade
lines.desc: A brass pin-tumbler door key: round bow with a hole, shoulder, blade with a milled groove and five V cuts whose depths (1 … 6) are its code; lying flat or held on edge ready to go into a lock. anchors: ring tip

lines.name: breadboard
lines.sig: breadboard cx cy k lab=0 lit=board|strips|rails
lines.desc: A white solderless breadboard (830 holes at 2.54 mm): terminal strips a–e and f–j either side of a centre channel, red + and blue − power rails along both edges; a bench part that resistors, capacitors, switches and leads plug into. anchors: top plus minus a1 j1

lines.name: breadloaf
lines.sig: breadloaf cx cy k lab=0 lit=loaf|bag
lines.desc: A sliced bread loaf, 25 × 12 × 12 cm, in a clear bag with a twist tie; a basic grocery item to price or put in a basket. anchors: top

lines.name: breaker
lines.sig: breaker cx cy height trip=N lab=1 lit=main|N
lines.desc: Home breaker panel with its door open: main switch, ten numbered breakers and the circuit directory; a tripped breaker sits in the middle with a red window, and the reset is fully OFF, then ON.

lines.name: brickwall
lines.sig: brickwall cx cy k w=100..300 h=60..200 aim=x|y move=-500..500 lab=0 lit=bricks|footing|coping
lines.desc: A free-standing brick wall in English bond on a concrete footing, with mortar joints, a damp-proof course and a concrete coping; runs along x or y, slides to set a distance (an echo wall, a wall to see over). anchors: face top

lines.name: bridge
lines.sig: bridge cx cy width k=beam|arch|suspension|cable|truss forces=1 truck=0..1 load=40 lab=1 lit=deck|piers|abutments|arch|towers|cables|anchor|truss
lines.desc: A museum model of a river crossing in five kinds (beam, arch, suspension, cable-stayed, truss); a lorry drives across and, with forces on, each member shows compression (red) or tension (blue) and the deck sags.

lines.name: bucket
lines.sig: bucket cx cy k water=0..1 lab=0 lit=bucket|handle|water
lines.desc: A 12 L plastic bucket with a steel wire handle and grip, litre marks inside and water up to `water` × its depth; a part to place in any scene. anchors: rim

lines.name: building
lines.sig: building cx cy width k=house|factory|shop|bank open=0..1 lights=0|1 lab=1 |sign lit=walls|windows|roof|chimney|sign|awning|columns
lines.desc: A house, factory, shop or bank built as the real thing: walls, windows, roof and door; open opens its door or rolls up its shutter, lights lights the windows.

lines.name: bulb
lines.sig: bulb cx cy height k=on|off power=0-100 out=0|1 lab=1 lit=glass|filament|cap|contact|switch
